yakone_goes_on_trial_over_international_.title: Yakone goes on trial over International Port bombing that killed 23, including a city councilor
yakone_goes_on_trial_over_international_.html:
Yakone, a Harbor Ward shipping broker, went on trial at the Republic City Circuit Court on Monday, charged with conspiracy and 23 counts of murder over the 14 May bombing at the International Port.

Deputy District Attorney Lian Okoro told the jury that Yakone arranged the delivery of the device to Pier Nine and the payments that funded it. He pleaded not guilty.

What happened

The explosion tore through a bonded warehouse on Pier Nine at 6:40 p.m., as dock crews were changing shifts. The Harbor Authority and Republic City General Hospital each put the dead at 23, including Councilor Shen Yiran of the Harbor Ward, who was at the pier to inspect a customs delay. Another 61 people were injured.

Police recovered a leaflet from the debris carrying a Salvationist slogan. No group has claimed responsibility.

The prosecution’s case

Okoro told the court that the device used a timer of Qianchan manufacture, and that a Qianchan trading house, Zhao-Meng and Sons, wired $140,000 to Yakone’s brokerage in the six weeks before the blast. He said the money was passed on to “persons who call themselves Salvationists.”

Okoro did not say what Qianchan would gain. He told the jury the state would show “who paid, not why.”

The Qianchan consulate told the Daily on Friday that it “has no knowledge of the firm’s accounts and rejects any suggestion of state involvement.” Zhao-Meng and Sons did not respond to requests for comment.

The defense

Yakone’s counsel, Marguerite Daw, told the jury the leaflet was printed on cheap paper available in any ward and that the Salvationist name was “put on this case in the first hour, and no one has asked since who wanted it there.” She said the transfers were routine payments for cargo insurance.

Councilor Shen was a vocal critic of the port’s brokerage fees. Daw said her client had lost business because of her and had no reason to kill her.

What’s next

Judge Rafael Imura said the trial is expected to run three weeks. The jury was seated on Friday after two days of questioning.

yakone_trial_everything_you_need_to_know.title: Yakone trial nears jury; Defense rests after 9 months
yakone_trial_everything_you_need_to_know.html:
The trial of Yakone, a Harbor Ward shipping broker accused of arranging the 14 May bombing at the International Port, enters its last stretch this week. Closing arguments are due Wednesday, and the jury of twelve is expected to begin deliberating by the weekend.

The case has moved faster than any terrorism trial the Republic has held: 273 days from the blast to a jury. It has also stalled once, for ten weeks, over a dispute with a foreign consulate. Both facts matter to how it ends.

What happened at Pier Nine

At 6:40 p.m. on 14 May 126 AG, as dock crews changed shifts, a bomb destroyed a bonded warehouse on Pier Nine. The Harbor Authority and Republic City General Hospital each count 23 dead. Another 61 were injured.

Among the dead was Councilor Shen Yiran of the Harbor Ward, who had gone to the pier to inspect a customs delay. Shen was a vocal critic of brokerage fees at the port. A Salvationist leaflet was recovered from the debris. No group claimed responsibility.

Timeline

14 May 126 AG: Bomb destroys the Pier Nine warehouse.

2 June: Yakone is arrested at his brokerage office on Anchor Row.

21 June: A grand jury indicts him on conspiracy and 23 counts of murder.

5 September: The jury is seated after two days of questioning.

8 September: Trial opens before Judge Rafael Imura.

26 September: Ren Kaito, a former courier for Salvationist remnants, testifies under a plea agreement.

3 October: The court recesses for ten weeks after the Qianchan consulate contests a subpoena for the records of Zhao-Meng and Sons.

12 January 127 AG: Hearings resume.

28 January: The defense rests after Yakone testifies for two days.

Who’s who

Yakone, 43. A shipping broker with an office on Anchor Row. He pleaded not guilty.

Judge Rafael Imura. Presiding. He denied the defense’s request for a mistrial in November.

Deputy District Attorney Lian Okoro. Leads the prosecution. She called 41 witnesses.

Marguerite Daw. Leads the defense. She called nine.

Ren Kaito. The state’s cooperating witness, a former Salvationist courier.

Zhao-Meng and Sons. A Qianchan trading house. The state says it wired the money.

The prosecution’s case

Okoro told the jury the case rests on three things.

The money. Records show $140,000 wired from Zhao-Meng and Sons to Yakone’s brokerage in the six weeks before the blast. A forensic accountant testified that the payments matched no cargo shipped through the port.

The timer. A fragment recovered from Pier Nine was of Qianchan manufacture. An ordnance expert said it was “not a part you buy by accident.”

The man. Ren testified that he picked up cash from Yakone’s office in April and delivered it to a man he knew only as “the Quartermaster.” A dock gate logbook placed Yakone near Pier Nine two days before the blast.

The defense’s case

Counsel Marguerite Daw told the jury the leaflet was printed on paper “sold in every ward in this city,” and that the Salvationist name was “put on this case in the first hour.” She said the transfers were cargo insurance premiums, and that Ren “traded a name for a deal.”

She also said Councilor Shen’s work against the brokers gave a number of people reason to want her gone, and that no one has found the Quartermaster.

The Salvationist question

By 126 AG, the Salvationists were a post-war remnant, and nothing in the evidence ties the bombing to an organized group with a name. The prosecution says the cell was small, three or four people, and the leaflet was theirs. The defense says the label let the case be built backward from a villain.

The Qianchan question

Qianchan has said the case “concerns a private firm.” The consulate fought the subpoena for Zhao-Meng’s records on grounds of commercial privilege, and the court ordered limited production. That fight caused the October recess. Neither Qianchan nor the firm has been charged.

Okoro told reporters last week that the state “is considering its options” on the indictment. She did not say what that meant.

What is not in dispute

The blast, the 23 dead, and that the money moved. What it was for is the case.

What the jury must decide

Twelve people must unanimously decide whether Yakone arranged the bombing and funded it. If they convict, the maximum sentence is life imprisonment, since the United Republic has no death penalty. If they cannot agree, the judge may declare a mistrial and the state may retry.

Legal scholars say the speed helped the state. “The evidence was fresh and no witness had time to forget,” said Prof. Imelda Varga of the Republic City University law faculty. Defense lawyers say it left no time to test the Qianchan records.

What to watch

Wednesday: Closing arguments.

Friday: Deliberations begin.

After a verdict: The Harbor Ward’s vacant council seat, empty since the blast, can go to a special election.

The Daily draws on court filings and public hearings. Mr. Yakone’s counsel and the Qianchan consulate were offered a chance to comment on this explainer; neither replied.

yakone_shot_by_squad_in_public_square_ri.title: Yakone shot by squad in public square; riots spread across city, 7 dead
yakone_shot_by_squad_in_public_square_ri.html:
Yakone, the Harbor Ward shipping broker convicted in the bombing of the International Port, was put to death by firing squad before several thousand persons in Republic Square yesterday morning, and within two hours the Lowtide district, where he was held by many to be a benefactor, was in flames.

Seven persons were dead last night, according to both the Republic City police and General Hospital. Police said 96 were injured, 23 of them officers; hospital officials said they had treated 143. Police said 412 persons had been arrested.

The execution

Mr. Yakone, 43, was shot at 7:04 a.m. by a squad of the Republic Guard, the first execution carried out under the treason clause of the Charter. A physician and a court officer were present, as the statute requires. The presidency said he was pronounced dead at 7:12 a.m., after the squad had fired twice.

Three persons who stood near the front of the crowd told a reporter that Mr. Yakone was still on his feet after the first volley. A spokesman for the presidency said that was untrue and that the sentence "was carried out in accordance with law." Neither account could be confirmed.

He had been convicted April 1 of treason, conspiracy and 23 counts of murder. The Supreme Court upheld the sentence May 28, four justices to one, and the President refused clemency June 5.

Weeks of vigils

For three weeks before the execution, crowds had gathered each evening in Lowtide, a district of tenements behind the harbor, and chanted for his release. After the President's refusal the chant changed. "He did nothing wrong," they said. Candles were set out on the steps of the Tenants' Council hall on Tide Street. The police made no arrests at the vigils.

The government dismissed the gatherings as the work of Salvationists. Police Commissioner Dessa Whitlock said June 10 that leaflets bearing Salvationist slogans had been found at three of them. Orrin Pell, chairman of the Tenants' Council, denied it. "They hand out a leaflet and say it's us," he said. "We lit candles."

The disorder

The first fires were set on Tide Street at about 9 a.m., as persons who had watched the execution returned to the district. By noon the crowds had moved toward the Harbor Ward and the Square, where Guard reservists were posted.

"They shot him and he was still standing," said Maren Kolb, 24, a Lowtide resident who said she was in the Square. "Then they shot him again. Nobody who saw that is going to be told it was Salvationists."

Commissioner Whitlock described the disorder last night as "organized violence by persons exploiting a lawful sentence," and said leaflets had again been found in the debris. Mr. Pell said the violence began "when the police charged a crowd that was kneeling." The police did not respond to that statement.

A curfew was imposed last night in Lowtide, the Harbor Ward, the Market District and the Old Quay, to run from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. The City Council will meet in emergency session tomorrow.

The Daily could not independently confirm the number of arrests, the early accounts of the execution, or the origin of the first fires. Mr. Yakone's family declined to comment.

bomb_wrecks_pier_nine_at_least_21_dead.title: Bomb wrecks pier nine; At least 21 dead
bomb_wrecks_pier_nine_at_least_21_dead.html:
A bomb tore through a bonded warehouse on Pier Nine of the International Port at 6:40 p.m. yesterday, killing at least 21 persons and injuring more than 40, among them Councilwoman Shen Yiran of the Harbor Ward, who was reported dead at the scene.

Harbor Authority officials put the dead at 21 last night. Physicians at Republic City General Hospital said two more of the injured, both burned, were not expected to live. No one has claimed responsibility.

The scene

The explosion came as the day crews were leaving and the night shift was coming on, when, Harbormaster Aldous Pryce said, "the pier is as full as it ever gets." The roof of the warehouse fell into the building and a fire burned for nearly three hours along the eastern quay.

"There was a flash, and then there was no sound at all, and then everybody was screaming," said Tomas Reyes, 34, a checker who was at the gate. "I saw men carrying other men out of it. I didn't see who was who."

Miss Shen, 51, had gone to the pier to look into a delay in the clearing of customs. She was in the warehouse office when the bomb went off, according to a clerk who survived.

Police inquiry

Police Commissioner Dessa Whitlock said a printed leaflet bearing a Salvationist slogan was found in the wreckage. She said it was too early to say what it meant. "It may have been left there or it may have been brought there by someone with a reason," she said. She would not say whether the police believed the explosion was connected to the unrest in Lowtide.

The Commissioner said the pier had been sealed and that the Guard bomb squad was searching the other warehouses.

The Relief Act

The blast came three weeks after the Republic Council passed the Public Relief and Housing Act, 7 to 4, on April 22. The law lays a levy on brokerage fees and bonded storage at the port, to pay for tenement repairs and weekly relief to poor households in Lowtide and other districts.

Miss Shen sponsored the measure and spoke for it on the floor. "The port grows rich on the backs of the people who live behind it," she said at the final reading.

The Harbor Brokers' Association opposed the act and has said it will challenge it in the courts. The association's chairman said last night that its members "deplore this act of violence and wish to be clear that it was not theirs."

Unrest in Lowtide

Crowds gathered in Lowtide on May 2 and 3 when the clerks opened the relief rolls. Tenants said the rolls, which require proof of residence, would be used to evict those who could not produce it. Police said stones were thrown on Tide Street and that shop windows were broken. Eighty-eight persons were arrested and 14 injured, among them six officers. The charges against most were later dropped.

The Council has said the rolls will not be used to evict anyone. The disorders had ended by May 5, the police said.

The dead

Among those identified last night were Councilwoman Shen, Harbor Authority clerk Anselm Rudd, stevedore Marcus Oyelaran, and dock foreman Teodor Wen. The Authority has asked families of workers who have not been accounted for to report to the Harbor Authority office on Anchor Row.

The Council will meet in special session this morning.

The Daily was unable to reach the Brokers' Association's chairman for further comment. The names of other victims are being withheld until families are notified.

the_law_permits_it_the_street_does_not.title: The law permits it; The street does not
the_law_permits_it_the_street_does_not.html:
The Republic Council has passed a law, and part of the city has answered it with stones. This newspaper has no wish to make light of what lies behind the stones. It has read the Act, it has read the Charter, and it has walked Tide Street. It concludes that the Act is lawful, that it is in the main wise, and that the disorders of last weekend were the fault of the persons who committed them and of no one else.

What the Act does

The Public Relief and Housing Act, passed by the Council 7 to 4 on April 22, does two things. It lays a levy on brokerage fees and bonded storage at the port, and with the proceeds it provides weekly relief to poor households and repairs to the tenements. That part has been argued about, chiefly by the Harbor Brokers' Association, but has not been much quarrelled with in the streets.

The second part has been. Part Four of the Act, headed Resettlement and Redevelopment, authorizes the Council to clear certain blocks of the Lowtide district and to transfer the households living there, at the Republic's expense, to the redevelopment quarter at Yu Dao or to housing in other districts of the country. The cleared ground will be paved for the new Hall of Records and for the Founders' Memorial, a monument to the Charter, which the Council has voted to raise on the site of Tide Street.

Notices were served on April 28. The first transfers are set for June 1. Each household is to receive a resettlement grant, passage for its goods, and the right to apply for a place in the new housing at Yu Dao, where building has gone on for three years.

What the Charter says

It is the practice of those who dislike a law to say that it offends the Charter. This newspaper has looked for the offense and cannot find it.

Article II gives the Council power "to legislate for the general welfare of the Republic." Article IV protects the home and the holding of every citizen, and in the same breath says that no person shall be deprived of either "except by law, for a public purpose, and upon just compensation." The same Article guarantees freedom of residence, and adds that this freedom is "subject to such laws as the Council may enact for the public welfare."

Here is the whole matter. The Act is a law. The Hall of Records and the Memorial are public purposes, and one may think the Memorial an extravagance without thinking it an unlawful one. The Act provides compensation, which the Council may enlarge but which no court has yet called unjust. Nothing in the Charter forbids the Republic to move people in order to build for the nation, and the Framers, who had lived through the clearing of the old Yanakawan quarters, knew very well what they were permitting. They permitted it with conditions. The Act meets them.

The grievance, fairly stated

This is not to say that those who live on Tide Street have nothing to complain of. A man who has lived all his life in one street, and been told that the street will be a monument, may be forgiven some bitterness. That the monument is to the Charter, which he is told protects his home, is an irony no committee of the Council foresaw and one the neighborhood has not missed.

Miss Shen Yiran, who sponsored the Act and spoke for it on the floor, has called resettlement "a ladder and not an exile." It may be. It will not look like a ladder to a widow of seventy who is asked to leave a place where she buried her husband and begin again in a quarter she has never seen. The Council would do well to remember that a law may be lawful and still be hard.

The disorders

It is the answer to the Act, however, that this newspaper must question. On May 2 and 3, crowds in Lowtide threw stones on Tide Street and broke the windows of shops. Eighty-eight persons were arrested and fourteen injured, six of them officers. The police say the disorders had ended by the 5th.

It would be convenient for the opponents of the Act to say that these were the Act's doing. They were not. The notices were served on April 28. No household had been moved. No house had been touched. Not one block had been cleared, and not one family had set foot at Yu Dao. The disorders came before the thing they were said to resist had begun.

Nor were they confined to Lowtide. In the same days there was trouble at Yu Dao itself, which is to receive the transferred, and at Gaipan and Awazu. secret_police_stood_by_as_empress_was_ki.title: Secret Police Stood By as Empress Was Killed, Sources Say; Group Behind Attack Still Unnamed
secret_police_stood_by_as_empress_was_ki.html:
Agents of the Dai Li, the Earth Kingdom's secret police, who were posted along the parade route and in the square yesterday, did not intervene when a bomb killed Empress Hou-Ting and stood by through the first minutes of the fighting, according to three people with knowledge of the security arrangements.

One of the three, a senior army officer, went further, saying the agency may have had a hand in the attack. That claim could not be verified, and the other two sources said they had no evidence of it. No one has claimed responsibility for the killing, and the group behind it has not been named.

Watching From the Sidelines

The three, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the state of emergency, said Dai Li agents were stationed on rooftops and in the colonnade along the length of the parade route and had been given responsibility for the Empress's immediate security. The Garrison and the Royal Guard were responsible for the crowds.

According to a palace official, the agents "did not move" for several minutes after the bomb was thrown at the Empress's motorcade. A second source, a Garrison officer, said the agents later withdrew to the Upper Ring palace compound rather than join the fighting in the Square, which lasted through the night.

The army officer said that Captain Kuvira Beifong of the 85th Infantry Division, who coordinated the units that retook the city, asked the Dai Li for help and received no reply. The Daily could not reach Captain Beifong.

An Allegation

The army officer said the parade route had been changed at the last moment, bringing the motorcade within range of the crowd, and that the change was ordered by the Dai Li. He offered no documents. A Royal Guard source said he knew of a route change but not who had ordered it.

Several people close to the court said the Empress had in recent months grown wary of the agency. The Empress, the daughter of King Kuei, took the throne in 153 AG after her father's death, which the court described at the time as natural.

The Attackers

No one has established who set off the bomb. At a press conference yesterday, military officials said they had seen increased anarchist and Equalist activity in the weeks beforehand, and some sources have linked the attack to the Red Lotus. They offered no evidence for either.

The rebels who fought the Garrison were equipped with advanced weapons and with mechanized suits from the Hundred Year War, officials said. The Garrison did not explain how such arms had reached the city.

The Dai Li's Reply

The Dai Li did not respond to written questions delivered to its compound on Tuesday night, and a person who answered the door said no one was available to speak. The agency has not made a public statement since the attack.

The Royal Council said it would announce its decision on the succession later today.

The Daily offered the Dai Li an opportunity to reply to each point in this report. The accounts of the three sources could not be independently confirmed, and the allegation about the route change is reported as made.

ba_sing_se_in_turmoil_after_empress_s_ki.title: Ba Sing Se in Turmoil After Empress’s Killing; Crowds Defy Troops as Armored Suits Roll Out
ba_sing_se_in_turmoil_after_empress_s_ki.html:
Crowds chanting against the government filled the streets of the Lower and Middle Rings of this capital for most of the day, and the Garrison, which said tonight it had regained the Square and the Upper Ring, put helicopters over the city and old armored suits from the Hundred Year War into the streets in an effort to quiet them.

The disorder followed the killing this morning of Empress Hou-Ting by a bomb thrown at her motorcade. It has left much of the capital under a state of emergency, with fires burning in at least four districts at the hour of filing.

Crowds and Chants

By early afternoon, the first crowds had gathered on Cauldron Street in the Lower Ring, and by 4 p.m. they numbered in the thousands. They did not chant for the Empress. "Who let them in?" they shouted at lines of troops, and, again and again, "Where were the guards?"

The question was a pointed one. At a press conference this afternoon, military officials acknowledged that warnings of increased Equalist and anarchist activity in the city had not been acted on in the weeks before the attack. They did not say why.

"They knew," said Bo Zhen, 52, a porter, standing near a barricade of overturned carts. "They are going to say they didn't, and then they are going to find a poor man to blame."

Offices Burned, Shops Looted

The crowds turned toward symbols of money by evening. The headquarters of the Earth Kingdom Rail Company, on Plum Avenue, was burning when this correspondent passed it at 7:30 p.m., and the offices of the Jade Lantern Insurance Company were gutted. The Middle Ring branch of the Royal Credit Bank was broken open and looted, and a grain syndicate's warehouse was emptied by crowds who carried the sacks away on their backs.

Nearby, in the Exchange district, smoke rose from the new Exchange building, which was struck by two explosions at about 6:15 p.m. Residents said the fire brigades could not get through.

Helicopters and Suits

Four helicopters of the Garrison's air wing began circling the Lower Ring at about 6 p.m., with loudspeakers that told the crowds to "return to your homes; the Kingdom stands." Leaflets with the same message were dropped over the Middle Ring.

At about 8 p.m., three of the heavy mechanized suits that were used in the Hundred Year War were brought down to an intersection on Cauldron Street from the Upper Ring armory, according to a Garrison officer, who asked not to be named. Rebels were also reported to have used suits of the same kind in last night's fighting. This correspondent saw no suit fire its weapons.

The effect on the crowd was mixed. Those in the front rows sat down in the street. Further back, bricks were thrown, and a bottle shattered against the leg of one suit. Many in the crowd, which was thinning by 9 p.m., said they had never seen the machines except in pictures.

The Count

The Garrison Command put the number killed in the capital at 23. The Lower Ring Free Clinic, which has been treating the wounded in its courtyard, said it had recorded 31. Neither figure could be confirmed.

A Garrison spokesman, Major Jiang Tao, said the Square and the Upper Ring had been "secured," and that order in the other rings would be restored by morning. The succession has not been announced.

The Daily offered the Garrison Command an opportunity to respond to the account of the helicopters and suits; Major Jiang's statement is reproduced above. This dispatch was filed from the Middle Ring.

exchange_ends_first_session_at_the_lowes.title: Exchange Ends First Session at the Lowest Level in Its History; Building Damaged by Blasts
exchange_ends_first_session_at_the_lowes.html:
The Ba Sing Se Exchange closed its first session yesterday at the lowest level in its history, which was also its only level, and remained shut this morning after two explosions damaged the building in the night of fighting that followed the death of Empress Hou-Ting.

The Exchange's chairman, Hong Bai, and its registrar, Lun Fei, each told the Times that the all-share index, set at 1,000 at the opening bell, stood at 660 when trading was halted at 10:40 a.m. No further trades were made. Both said the Exchange would not reopen until the state of emergency was lifted.

A Public Exchange, for One Morning

The Exchange opened yesterday as the first in the Earth Kingdom to admit any adult citizen as an investor, replacing the old Bourse, which was limited to members. It had been timed to coincide with the founding-day celebrations. Mr. Hong said about 3,000 people were in the building at the opening.

The Empress was killed at about 9:20 a.m., when a bomb was thrown at her motorcade in Ba Sing Se Square. Mr. Lun said the first sale orders arrived within five minutes. "There were no buyers at any price," he said.

The Night's Damage

Two explosions struck the Exchange building at about 6:15 p.m., according to Mr. Hong, who said he was in a nearby street at the time. Part of the trading floor is open to the sky, and the records office is burned.

The Garrison Command, through its spokesman, Major Jiang Tao, put the number of dead near the Exchange at 11. The figure is the Garrison's and has not been checked against hospital records. Major Jiang said the district had been cleared at about 1:30 a.m. by units under Captain Kuvira Beifong of the 85th Infantry Division. He did not say who set off the explosions or whether the building had been targeted.

Banks and the Currency

The Central Bank said last night that all banks would remain closed under the emergency order. A bank officer, who asked not to be named, said depositors had begun queuing at some branches on the Lower Ring before the news of the Empress's death was widely known.

The Qianchan Treasury said Earth Kingdom paper was trading at a discount of about 30 percent in Gaoling. The Times could not confirm that figure independently.

The Government

The succession remains undecided, and no member of the royal household or the Royal Council has spoken publicly since the attack. Officials of the Council said an announcement was expected later today. The city is under curfew, and parts of the capital were still burning at the hour of filing.

ba_sing_se_exchange_plunges_on_opening_d.title: Ba Sing Se Exchange Plunges on Opening Day After Empress Is Killed; Bombs Hit Trading Floor
ba_sing_se_exchange_plunges_on_opening_d.html:
The Ba Sing Se Exchange, which opened to the public for the first time this morning, collapsed within an hour of the news that Empress Hou-Ting had been killed by a bomb, and was struck by two explosions in the evening as fighting spread through the capital.

Exchange officials said prices fell 34 percent between the opening bell and a halt at 10:40 a.m. Trading did not resume. Fighting was continuing near the palace district at the hour of filing.

An Opening Day Cut Short

The Exchange was to be the showpiece of the founding-day celebrations. It replaces the old Ba Sing Se Bourse, which was open only to members, and the Empress's government had promised that it would for the first time let any citizen buy shares. About 3,000 people were in the building when the bell rang, an Exchange spokesman said.

The Empress was killed at about 9:20 a.m., when a bomb was thrown at her motorcade during the parade in Ba Sing Se Square. Word reached the trading floor within minutes. "Every order was a sell order," said a clerk reached by telephone, who gave his name as Wen. "There was no one left to buy."

Bombs at the Exchange

Two explosions hit the Exchange building at about 6:15 p.m., according to residents of the district. A garrison spokesman said at least 11 people were killed and that the figure could not be confirmed. Fire crews were unable to reach the building.

The garrison said armed rebels had been moving through the district. It did not say who they were, and it had not established whether the Exchange was a target or was caught in the fighting.

A Flight to Safety

In Gaoling, shares fell 9 percent at the opening of trading, according to the Gaoling Exchange. The Qianchan note rose 4 percent against Earth Kingdom paper, and the price of gold reached a record on the Gaoling market.

The Treasury of the Republic of Qianchan said it was "monitoring the situation closely." Mei-Lin Hao, who has traded on the Gaoling floor for 41 years, said the day recalled the crash of 153 AG. "That one took a week to get going," she said. "This one took an hour."

The Qianchan foreign ministry said it was checking on its nationals in Ba Sing Se. Among those reported to have taken part in the defense of the Square was Captain Kuvira Beifong of the Earth Kingdom's 85th Infantry Division, who also holds Qianchan citizenship.

Figures are from the Ba Sing Se and Gaoling exchanges and the Qianchan Treasury. The Ba Sing Se casualty count could not be confirmed.

stocks_plunge_around_the_world_exchanges.title: Stocks Plunge Around the World; Exchanges Halt Trading
stocks_plunge_around_the_world_exchanges.html:
Stock prices collapsed on exchanges around the world on Monday and Tuesday, forcing the Republic City Exchange and three others to suspend trading, as the failure of a major Caldera lending house and doubt over who will succeed King Kuei of the Earth Kingdom shook confidence in every market that deals across the oceans.

By the close yesterday, the Caldera Exchange was down 31 percent over two sessions, according to its officials. The Republic City Exchange had lost 22 percent, and the Ba Sing Se Bourse, which closed for two days, was reported down more than a quarter. It was the sharpest fall in stock prices anywhere since the end of the civil war.

The Lender That Failed

The first blow came on Sunday, Sept. 27, when the Hakuryu Trust, a Caldera house that had lent heavily against cargoes of rice and shipping contracts, told its creditors it could not meet its obligations. The Trust is owed, by its own account, the equivalent of several years' revenue of the Caldera harbor.

riots_erupt_in_joha_after_dock_workers_m.title: Riots Erupt in Joha After Dock Workers’ March; 3 Dead
riots_erupt_in_joha_after_dock_workers_m.html:
Rioting broke out in the port city of Joha yesterday afternoon after police broke up a march of dock workers, leaving three people dead and dozens injured and prompting the prefectural government to impose a curfew on the harbor district.

The disorder, the worst in Joha since the end of the civil war, came less than two weeks after the sharpest fall in stock prices on the Caldera Exchange in a generation, and less than two months after the death of King Kuei of the Earth Kingdom, whose passing has brought leftist groups back into the streets in several cities.

A March Turns Violent

The march was organized by the Joha Dockworkers' Union to mourn the king and to press a claim for back pay that the union says the harbor's employers have owed since the port was rebuilt. Union officials put the crowd at about 6,000. The police said it was nearer 4,000.

The marchers were to have gone from the union hall to the quay memorial. Police stopped them at the Customs Road crossing at about 2 p.m., saying the union had no permit for the route. Witnesses said a line of officers with shields moved forward, bottles and stones were thrown, and the police fired into the crowd.

Three people were killed, according to both the police and the union. Joha Municipal Hospital said it treated 52 injured, among them 19 police officers. The police said 140 persons were arrested.

By evening, crowds had broken shop windows along Customs Road and set fire to a freight office on the eastern quay. Fire crews were kept from the quay until after 9 p.m.

"We marched for a dead king and for our wages," said Haruki Nomura, the union's secretary. "Nobody told us the police had a different march in mind."

Police Commissioner Rin Katsura said officers "acted when the order of the street was lost." He said he could not yet say who threw the first stone. "That will be established," he said.

The Exchange and the Docks

The anger in Joha has an economic root that predates the march. Prices on the Caldera Exchange fell 31 percent over two sessions on Sept. 28 and 29, according to exchange officials, and trading was suspended for a day. Shipping and shipbuilding shares, which had led the rise of recent years, fell hardest.

Two Joha companies, a shipping line and a yard, laid off 2,300 workers on Oct. 5, the union said. Neither company confirmed the number. "It was the worst two days since the war," said Keiji Arai, a professor of economics at Caldera University. "The question for Joha is whether it was a market correction or the start of a long slide."

Ito Matsuda, 38, a rigger, said he lost his job on Monday. "They owed us for the rebuilding and now they say there is no money at all," he said, standing near the freight office after the fire. "What do you want a man to do?"

A Name With a History

Joha carries a weight that other ports do not. The Salvationist movement held its first mass gatherings on the city's quay in the last years of the Hundred Year War, and residents still call it the blood city, after a shooting there in July 100 AG. Many of those on the march had their own memories of that day, or their parents'.

Governor Genji Hoshino did not link yesterday's events to the Salvationists. "Order will be kept in this city," he said in a statement. "Those who broke it will answer to the law."

Commissioner Katsura said handbills from leftist groups not previously active in Joha had been found among the marchers, but he declined to say what the groups were. Mr. Nomura said the handbills had been handed out by "people the union did not invite."

The Curfew

The Governor's office said a curfew would be in force in the harbor district from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. until further notice. Schools in the district were closed for the day.

The Diet is to take up the matter on Monday. The Royal Household Office had no comment.

This article is based on interviews with 14 people in Joha, and on figures supplied by Joha Municipal Hospital and the prefectural police. The Scire could not independently confirm the size of the crowd or who threw the first stone.

unrest_grips_joha_cradle_of_salvationist.title: Unrest Grips Joha, Cradle of Salvationists, as Fire Lord Stays Out of Sight
unrest_grips_joha_cradle_of_salvationist.html:
For more than a year, strikes and riots have spread from the port city of Joha across the surrounding prefecture, and now the Fire Lord, Zuko, has not been seen in public since he visited here on Sept. 11. Officials will not say where he is.

The Royal Household Office said on Sept. 14 that the Fire Lord was resting on the advice of his physicians, and that "certain disturbances" in Joha were the work of Salvationist sympathizers. It gave no date for his return.

Official statement. Royal Household Office, Sept. 14, 154 AG (abridged): "His Majesty is resting at a residence of the Household on the advice of his physicians. He has not cancelled his obligations to Tajisaki and will resume them when the physicians permit."

The statement, and the silence around it, have left this port of about 400,000 people under curfews that cover four of the prefecture's six districts, with the dead counted in two ways by two authorities and no explanation of the difference.

A Spreading Unrest

The trouble began in August 1953 AG, within days of the death of King Kuei of the Earth Kingdom. Leftist groups that had been quiet since the civil war held rallies in several cities, among them Caldera City. In Joha, dock workers marched on Oct. 9 to mourn the king and to demand pay they say they have been owed since the harbor was rebuilt.

Prefectural police broke up the march. Three people were killed, according to both the police and the Joha Dockworkers' Union. Larger marches followed on the next two Saturdays, and by December there were riots in the grain towns inland.

The "Blood City"

Joha is not a place where officials can claim surprise at a crowd. The Salvationist movement held its first mass gatherings on the city's quay in the last years of the Hundred Year War, and residents still call it the blood city. The name comes from a gathering there in July 100 AG, the week word of Emperor Ozai's death reached the coast, that ended in killings. Residents interviewed by the Scire disagree about who fired.

Governor Genji Hoshino said in an interview that the movement "has been dead for thirty years and is being dug up by people who never saw it." Police Commissioner Rin Katsura said a cache of weapons found in a warehouse in April, along with handbills carrying old Salvationist slogans, showed "someone is doing the digging on purpose."

The dockworkers' union rejects that account. Its secretary, Haruki Nomura, said the marches were organized by the union. "The Salvationists came later," he said, "and the Governor needs them to have come first."

Two Counts of the Dead

The prefectural police say 41 people have been killed since October 153 AG. Dr. Ayame Ōtsuka, director of Joha Municipal Hospital, said its records show 118 deaths from injuries and gunshot wounds over the same period.

Neither side has accounted for the difference. The Governor's office said the hospital's figure included "deaths from other causes during the curfew." Dr. Ōtsuka rejected that, saying each case is individually documented. The Scire has not been shown the hospital's records.

The question has reached the Diet. "The prefecture is being governed by curfew, and the Diet has not been told by whom," Daichi Mori, a member of the Reform bloc, said at a sitting on Sept. 2, according to the transcript.

The Fire Lord's Visit

The Fire Lord arrived in Joha on Sept. 11 in what officials described as an effort to calm the city. Accounts of what followed differ.

The Household Office says the visit was cut short because His Majesty grew tired. Two dock workers who were near the motorcade said it stopped at the quay memorial after a crowd surged forward, and that they heard shots. The police said they could not confirm that shots were fired. The Scire could not independently confirm either account.

Crown Princess Izumi has taken over the ceremonial duties of the throne. A sitting of the Diet that had been set for Sept. 16 was postponed, with no new date announced.

Unanswered Questions

The Household Office has not said where the Fire Lord is, what he is being treated for, or why the visit ended early. The prefectural government has not said who ordered the curfews, or under what authority.

The Scire asked the Household Office on Sept. 17 where the Fire Lord is resting and when he will resume his public duties. It had not replied by the time this article went to press.

This article is based on interviews with 23 people in Joha between Sept. 12 and 19, and on records supplied by the prefectural police and Joha Municipal Hospital. The casualty figures could not be reconciled.
